newsitem.title: MEXICO: Guatemalan stock exchange aims to grow - director.
newsitem.headline: Guatemalan stock exchange aims to grow - director.

text.p: Guatemala's 10-year old Bolsa de Valores Nacional, S.A. is aiming to grow, pulled ahead by a wave of structural reforms and a push to list new companies, Rolando San Roman, the director general of the stock exchange, said on Thursday.

The exchange, which has about 65 percent of the Guatemalan market, could benefit from a number of important changes, including the peace process in the Central American country and a better legal framework, he said in an interview.
Currently there are seven stocks listed on the Bolsa de Valores Nacional with a total market capitalization of about $140 million.
But among the other product listed there are also 140 companies who offer commercial paper, with maturities of up to five years.
"What we are aiming for is to help some of these 140 companies see the benefits of going public and to help them find funds for their development," San Roman said.
He was attending a conference of the International Federation of Stock Exchanges in this resort city.
Guatemala has also passed or is considering passing a number of new laws that will help to transform the economy.
A key one was the Securities Law, which provided a clearer legal foundation, including for the clearing and settlement system and rules on institutional investing.
The economy is also seen profiting from a number of political and economic events.
"We expect privatizations to heat up, multilateral assistance to increase to assist in the rebuilding, and private investment to rebound," Bankers Trust economist Carl Ross said in a recent report.

The hundreds of millions of dollars promised to Guatemala now that the umbrella guerrilla organization (URNG) and the government have signed a peace pact will eventually help rebuild the economy by working its way into infrastructure projects.
"It will have a direct impact on the infrastructure of the country," San Ramon said.
The government has also said it will sell-off the telephone company, which could possibly be listed on Guatemalan exchanges or even on foreign exchanges.
Rumours place the value of the privatization at about $1.0 billion.
Assets of the railway company and the national electrical company could also be sold.
The Guatemalan Congress will also have to decide on the fate of proposed private pension funds, based on the Chilean model.
"It could certainly give a big push to the development of the capital markets," San Ramon said about the proposed pension funds.
He noted that Guatemala's economy is improving, with government tax revenues increasing along with international reserves and exports.
The Bolsa de Valores Nacional is privately owned by its members and was incorporated in 1986.
Another exchange accounts for the remaining 35 percent of stocks traded in Guatemala.
((--Mexico City newsroom, 525 728-7902))
